standard.title: Causes and Outbreak of the Second World War
standard.description: the causes, outbreak and course of the Second World War and the significance of Australian involvement
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the causes and course of World War One at Year 9, including the alliance system, nationalism, imperialism, and the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand; the Western Front; the significance of Australian involvement including Gallipoli and the home front.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the causes and outbreak of the Second World War across European and Asia-Pacific contexts, analyse the course of the war, and evaluate the significance of Australian involvement.

nodes.label: Inter-war conditions as causes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how inter-war events and conditions — including the Treaty of Versailles, the Great Depression, and the rise of fascism and militarism — created the preconditions for the Second World War.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two inter-war causes from different domains (e.g. one economic, one political) and connect them to the outbreak of war.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the Treaty of Versailles (territorial concessions, war reparations), the structural weaknesses of the League of Nations, the Great Depression, the Russian Revolution, and the rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party from 1933; explain how these conditions interacted to create the conditions for war.
wider: Examine the role of the Great Depression in destabilising democratic governments and enabling extremist movements in multiple countries simultaneously, not only Germany
Investigate the ideological dimensions of interwar politics — comparing fascism, communism and liberal democracy as competing responses to post-WWI instability
Explore lesser-studied contributing causes such as the Italo-Abyssinian Wars or the Spanish Civil War as early demonstrations of fascist aggression and the limits of collective security
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat the war as caused by Hitler alone — rather than understanding the structural conditions that enabled his rise — will misread every subsequent cause-effect chain in the lead-up to war. The multi-causal framework built here underpins Nodes 2 and 3.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly collapse complex causation into single-cause explanations. Use structured cause-mapping (e.g. categorising causes as economic, political, ideological, structural) to build a multi-causal framework before asking students to weigh causes.

Extend the Treaty of Versailles analysis across multiple affected parties — Germany, Austria-Hungary successor states, colonial mandates — to show that the grievances enabling fascism were systemic, not unique to Germany.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The interwar period offers rich comparative width — students can examine how the same structural conditions (Depression, weak collective security, nationalist grievance) produced different political outcomes in different countries, building genuine historical reasoning about contingency and causation.
success_criteria: Identify at least two inter-war causes of WWII from different domains and explain the link between each cause and the eventual outbreak of war
Explain why the structural weaknesses of the League of Nations reduced the effectiveness of collective security in the 1930s
Describe the conditions that enabled the rise of the Nazi Party in Germany, connecting at least one economic and one political factor

nodes.label: Events leading to outbreak
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the major events in the lead-up to the outbreak of the Second World War, explaining how each contributed to the collapse of the international order.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse at least three major pre-war events (from either the European or Asia-Pacific theatre) and explain how each brought war closer.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the chain of major events leading to outbreak across both theatres: Japanese invasion of Manchuria, Spanish Civil War, Italo-Abyssinian Wars, annexation of Austria, Munich Agreement and Sudetenland, invasion of Poland (1939), occupation of China, and the attack on Pearl Harbor (1941); explain the failure of appeasement policy using Munich as a case study.
wider: Examine the Munich Agreement in depth as a case study in the failure of appeasement — analysing Chamberlain's reasoning, Hitler's response, and how historians have debated whether appeasement was inevitable or a strategic miscalculation
Compare the timeline of aggression in the European and Asia-Pacific theatres, examining whether the two paths to war were connected or largely independent until 1941
Investigate the role of public opinion and domestic politics in Britain and France in constraining governments' responses to fascist aggression in the 1930s

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of key pre-war events across both theatres. Use a chronological mapping task — students annotate each event with its theatrical context (European/Asia-Pacific), the aggressor, and the international response — before attempting causal analysis.

success_criteria: Sequence at least three major pre-war events correctly and explain how each contributed to the outbreak of war
Explain why the policy of appeasement failed, using the Munich Agreement as evidence
Identify at least one key event in each of the European and Asia-Pacific theatres that moved the world closer to war

nodes.label: Course of the war — theatres and turning points
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the course of the Second World War across the European and Asia-Pacific theatres, identifying its major phases.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the major phases of the war in at least one theatre (European or Asia-Pacific) and identify at least two turning-point events.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the major phases and turning points across both theatres: in Europe — Blitzkrieg, Battle of Britain, Operation Barbarossa, Operation Overlord, the fall of Berlin; in the Asia-Pacific — Pearl Harbor, fall of Singapore, Battle of Midway, island-hopping campaign; explain how momentum shifted over time.
wider: Examine the Eastern Front (Operation Barbarossa and its consequences) as the war's largest theatre by casualties, comparing its scale and significance with the Western Front narrative that dominates Australian textbooks

Investigate the role of technology and logistics (radar, code-breaking, supply chains) as determinants of turning-point events, examining how the war was shaped by industrial and scientific capability as much as military strategy

response_modes.reason: Students need a working knowledge of major events across both theatres as a foundation for the significance analysis in Node 4. Use visual timelines or map-based activities to build spatial and temporal orientation before asking for analysis.

success_criteria: Identify at least two turning-point events in the war and explain why each was significant
Describe the major phases of the war in at least one theatre in chronological sequence
Explain how the balance of power between the Allied and Axis powers shifted across the course of the war

nodes.label: Significance of Australian involvement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the significance of Australian involvement in the Second World War, including the decisions of Australian political leaders and Australia's strategic shift toward the United States.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why Australia joined the Second World War and evaluate the significance of at least one aspect of Australian involvement (e.g. the Menzies vs Curtin decisions, the Pacific theatre campaigns).
nodes.typical_width: Examine the reasons for Australia's involvement — including Menzies' 'Australia is also at war' and Curtin's 'Australia looks to America'; evaluate the significance of Australian campaigns in the Pacific (Kokoda, Milne Bay, New Guinea); explain how the war accelerated Australia's strategic reorientation from Britain to the USA.
wider: Evaluate the contrasting wartime leadership of Menzies and Curtin as a lens on how Australia's national identity and strategic priorities were contested and reshaped during the war

Compare Australia's strategic situation in 1942 with that of other British Dominions (Canada, New Zealand, South Africa), examining how each navigated the tension between Imperial loyalty and national interest

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the inter-war causes (Node 1), pre-war events (Node 2), and course of the war (Node 3) into a specific evaluative claim about Australian significance. Structured essay or analytical paragraph tasks work well here — students draw on the full knowledge base to support a position.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Menzies/Curtin contrast and Australia's strategic pivot offer rich opportunities to examine how domestic political leadership intersects with global events — a genuinely transferable historical thinking skill that extends well beyond the specific content.
success_criteria: Explain at least two reasons for Australia's decision to enter the Second World War
Evaluate the significance of at least one Australian military campaign, explaining what was at stake and what was achieved
Explain how the Second World War changed Australia's strategic relationship with Britain and the United States
